title: Apollo 11, Tranquility Base from orbit
summary: Eight stops over the Apollo 11 landing site seen from lunar orbit, from West crater down to the lander, its shadow, the experiments and Armstrong's trail, and how the sun's direction changes what you see.

stops.title: Tranquility Base
stops.body:
Apollo 11 landed here, in the Sea of Tranquility (Mare Tranquillitatis) on the Moon, at 20:17 UTC on 20 July 1969 (20:17:40, as LROC gives it).

NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter took this picture from orbit on 5 November 2011, with its two Narrow Angle Cameras. They record visible light in one broad band, so the picture is gray. One pixel covers 40 centimeters, and the view is about 1.74 kilometers on a side, north up. It was morning there: the sun shines from the east, the right.

validation.notes: Accepted with caveats by science review (reviewer, mathematician, physicist); fixes applied. docs/science/moon-apollo-11.md, Validation of J-01.

stops.title: West crater and the landing
stops.body: The big crater on the right is West crater, about 190 meters across. Eagle, the lunar module, was heading for a point on its rocky northeast side. Neil Armstrong saw the hazard, kept flying and set down about half a kilometer farther on, near the left of this view, just past a small crater later called Little West.

validation.notes: Accepted with caveats by science review (reviewer, mathematician, physicist); fixes applied. docs/science/moon-apollo-11.md, Validation of J-01.

stops.title: The descent stage
stops.body:
The bright square is the descent stage of Eagle, the lower half of the lunar module, which stayed on the Moon when the astronauts left. Its deck is 3.7 meters on a side, about 9 of the picture's pixels, and its top stands 3 meters above the ground. Each pixel covers 40 centimeters, the smallest detail this picture holds: zooming in further makes the pixels bigger but adds no detail.

The deck is so bright that it shows as plain white, with no detail. Its shadow falls just to the west, on the left. With the sun about 49 degrees above the horizon, we calculate it should reach only about 2.6 meters past the stage, under 10 of the picture's pixels.

validation.notes: Accepted with caveats by science review (reviewer, mathematician, physicist); fixes applied. docs/science/moon-apollo-11.md, Validation of J-01.

stops.title: The shadow flips
stops.body:
Drag the divider. The other picture shows the same place on 22 January 2011, in the afternoon. The sun was in the west and lower, about 27 degrees above the horizon, so the shadow falls to the east, on the other side of the lander, and is longer: more than twice as long, by our calculation from the sun's height.

The lander does not line up exactly across the divider: it shifts by about 1.3 meters while the ground around it matches. Its top is 3 meters above the ground, and the camera looked almost straight down in November but about 10 degrees off vertical in January; the sunlit side of the lander also switched sides. The ground alignment is not the cause.

sources.label: PDS Geosciences Orbital Data Explorer (ODE), LROC NAC M175124932 and M150361817

validation.notes: Accepted with caveats by science review (reviewer, mathematician, physicist); fixes applied. docs/science/moon-apollo-11.md, Validation of J-01.

stops.title: Experiments left behind
stops.body:
About 20 to 30 meters south of the lander are two experiments the astronauts set up, part of the Early Apollo Scientific Experiments Package. Each spans only a few of the picture's 40-centimeter pixels, so zooming in shows blocks of gray, not the shape of the instruments.

The northern one is the Laser Ranging RetroReflector, an array of small reflectors: laser pulses fired from Earth bounce off it, and their travel time measures the distance between Earth and the Moon. It still works, though dust has dimmed it. The southern one is the Passive Seismic Experiment Package. The dark ground around it comes from the astronauts' repeated footsteps.

sources.label: NASA SP-214, Apollo 11 Preliminary Science Report, ch. 7
Apollo 11 traverse map, LROC PDS volume

stops.title: A walk to Little West
stops.body:
A dark trail runs east from the lander for about 60 meters and stops at the rim of Little West crater, 40 meters across. Neil Armstrong walked out here to look at and photograph the crater during his time outside.

The trail is darker than the ground around it. At the Apollo 12 site the LROC team found the most-walked ground darkest, most likely because walking packed down the loose surface powder. The trails are still visible from orbit more than four decades later.

sources.label: Apollo 11 traverse map, LROC PDS volume

stops.title: Where did the trail go?
stops.body:
Drag the divider. In the January picture the trail is faint. In our reading of the two pictures it is still there: the light is different.

The trail differs from its surroundings mostly in brightness, and the LROC team found that astronaut paths stand out clearly when the sun is high and shadows are few. In January the sun was lower, so the shading of every bump and crater wall takes over the picture. The January picture also has coarser pixels, 0.5 meters against 0.4, and its own brightness scaling.

validation.notes: Accepted with caveats by science review (reviewer, mathematician, physicist); fixes applied. docs/science/moon-apollo-11.md, Validation of J-01.

stops.title: Your turn
stops.body: Drag to move and zoom in anywhere, and move the divider. Every small crater has a wall lit by the sun and a wall in shade, and they swap between the two pictures because the sun shone from opposite sides. Brightness cannot be compared: each picture was reduced to its own brightness scale. About ten months passed between the two, but what you see change is the light and the view, not the ground.
